| [NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md) | Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | The 2014 restatement of IIT. Five axioms of experience become five postulates about mechanisms in a state, and an experience is identified with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a complex. Exclusion is the anti-nesting rule: of all overlapping sets of elements, only the one with locally maximal Φ is conscious, so no subset or superset of a complex is. It is postulated from the axiom that experience has definite borders; Occam's razor is invoked only for exclusion within a mechanism. Logic-gate examples give minor complexes, a conscious inactive network, a minimally conscious photodiode and a feed-forward zombie. Nothing larger than about a dozen elements is computable. | Read |

| [NOTE-958](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-958.md) | Sandved-Smith et al. — computational phenomenology of mental action | A three-level discrete active-inference model in which attentional states set the precision of the perceptual likelihood and meta-awareness states set the precision of the attentional likelihood; mental action is a choice of 'stay' or 'switch' over attentional states, defined at the second level only, against a preference to observe oneself 'focused'. | [NOTE-1065](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1065.md) | Ward — What is enactivism? | A conceptual paper. The usual taxonomy, which lumps every view stressing sensorimotor loops as "enactivism" and splits it into autopoietic, sensorimotor and radical variants, hides what is distinctive about The Embodied Mind. A second axis, organicist against informationalist, runs across the cognitivist–embodied one. Enactivism is organicist, and it adds the primacy of lived experience and a reciprocity in which scientific vocabularies reshape the experience they describe. Most embodied views, predictive processing among them, are informationalist. It argues for a taxonomy, not for enactivism's truth. | Read |
| [NOTE-1070](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1070.md) | Woods, Windt & Carter — Contentless experiences in meditation are neither truly contentless nor identical | An evidence synthesis of 135 expert texts on the goal-states of Shamatha (Wallace), Transcendental Meditation and Stillness Meditation. It codes 65 features. The states are said to lack thoughts, concepts, perceptions, images and memories, but to keep wakefulness, calm, stillness, bliss, knowing, freedom, unity and more. They are the same across the practices on 14 features, different on 4 (chiefly Shamatha's far greater attentional stability and vividness) and unclear on 47. So, on the texts, they are neither truly contentless nor identical. The data are teachers' descriptions, not participants' reports. | Read |
| [NOTE-1163](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1163.md) | Isaac — Phenomenal structure: what is it and what is it for? | A structuralist programme for the science of phenomenal experience, set out as a stance and not a thesis. Experience has three layers of structure: quality-space geometry, which is a precondition for meaning; group-theoretic constancy, which "induces a distinction between subject and object"; and dynamic structure, vector fields of valence and affordance, which guide action. The method is the search for structure-preserving maps among experience, world and brain, held as a regulative ideal and advanced by de-idealizing the models where the maps fail. The evidence that such models target experience, not mere behaviour, is chiefly convergence between models built by different behavioural routes, which the paper admits is always partial. The group-theoretic and dynamic layers are, in the author's words, "mere suggestive sketches". | Read |
| [NOTE-1289](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1289.md) | Second-Person Engagement, Self-Alienation, and Group-Identification | A reconstruction and defence of Husserl's empathy-based account of the "we". Truly social acts need an I–Thou relation of reciprocal, communicative address, beyond even reciprocal empathy. In it I am aware of myself as addressed, and by taking over the other's perspective on me ("self-alienation") the self–other difference stays present but is "somewhat downplayed". That is a formal, necessary but not sufficient, condition of seeing oneself as one of us. "A we, a first-person plural, is not an enlarged I." Zahavi likens it to self-categorization theory's self-stereotyping, replies to Heidegger and Schmid that the "we" can be analysed and that self-awareness precedes in-group bias, and concedes that the face-to-face "we" does not cover anonymous ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1309](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1309.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | A we-identity is held as a group member, is at times salient, is endorsed, and varies in affective salience. Self-categorization theory explains we-identities by depersonalization: seeing oneself as an interchangeable exemplar of a prototype. Phenomenologists (Zahavi, Salice) have adopted it for the "we" in general. But close relationships, such as long friendships and partnerships, yield we-identities by mutual individualization, in which each grasps the other as non-substitutable. So depersonalization is not necessary for a we-identity. León sketches a socially extended account, drawing on Husserl and on extended-mind criteria. | Read |
| [NOTE-1434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1434.md) | Metzinger — Why are dreams interesting for philosophers? | Metzinger proposes that minimal phenomenal selfhood reduces to transparent spatiotemporal self-location, because people report a stable self in bodiless dreams and asomatic out-of-body experiences, located at an extensionless point without a body.
